modules.title: Getting Started
modules.subtitle: What Python is, your first program, input and syntax

lessons.title: What is Python?
lessons.summary: Meet the most popular programming language in the world and discover why developers, scientists and companies love it.

blocks.text: **Python** is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by **Guido van Rossum** and first released in 1991. It was designed to be easy to read — Python code often looks almost like plain English.
Why learn Python?

items: **Beginner friendly** — simple, clean syntax with no curly braces or semicolons.
**Huge community** — millions of developers and thousands of free libraries.
**Versatile** — web apps, data science, AI, automation, games, scripting and more.
**In demand** — one of the most requested skills in developer job listings.

blocks.text: Where is Python used?

items: **Web development** — Django, Flask and FastAPI power sites like Instagram and Pinterest.
**Data science & AI** — pandas, NumPy, TensorFlow and PyTorch.
**Automation** — scripts that rename files, send emails or scrape websites.
**Education & research** — the language of choice in many universities.

blocks.text: Python is an **interpreted** language: an interpreter reads your code line by line and runs it immediately. That's exactly what happens when you tap **Run** in the PyMaster terminal.
Your phone is running a real Python interpreter:
blocks.code:
import sys
print("Hello from Python!")
print("Python version:", sys.version.split()[0])

blocks.text: Python is named after the comedy group **Monty Python**, not the snake — but the snake logo stuck!

keyPoints: Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose language.
It is used for web, data science, AI, automation and much more.
Readable syntax makes it perfect for beginners and professionals.
lessons.practice: Open the terminal and run `print("I am learning Python!")`.

lessons.title: Your first program: print()
lessons.summary: The `print()` function displays text and values on the screen. It's the first tool every Python developer uses.

blocks.text: A **function** is a reusable piece of code that performs a task. `print()` is a built-in function that shows output. You put what you want to display inside the parentheses.

blocks.code:
print("Hello, World!")
print('Single quotes work too')
print(42)
print(3.14)
blocks.output:
Hello, World!
Single quotes work too
42
3.14

blocks.text: Printing several values
Separate values with commas. `print()` puts a space between them automatically.

blocks.code:
print("I am", 25, "years old")
print("Python", "is", "fun", sep="-")
print("No new line here", end=" ... ")
print("same line!")
blocks.output:
I am 25 years old
Python-is-fun
No new line here ... same line!

blocks.text: `sep` changes the separator between values and `end` changes what is printed at the end (a new line by default).
Empty lines

blocks.code:
print("Line 1")
print()
print("Line 3")

blocks.text: Text inside quotes is called a **string**. Without quotes, Python thinks it's a name of a variable or function.

keyPoints: Use commas to print several values separated by spaces.
`sep` sets the separator, `end` sets the line ending.
lessons.practice: Print your name, age and city on one line separated by ` | ` using the `sep` parameter.

lessons.title: Comments & clean code
lessons.summary: Comments explain your code to humans. Python ignores them completely.

blocks.text: A **comment** starts with `#`. Everything after `#` on that line is ignored by Python. Good comments explain **why** the code does something.

blocks.code:
# This program greets the user
print("Welcome!")  # comments can follow code too

# print("This line will not run")

blocks.text: Multi-line notes (docstrings)
Triple-quoted strings are often used as multi-line documentation, called **docstrings**.

blocks.code:
"""
Program: Greeter
Author:  PyMaster student
"""
print("Docstrings document your code")

blocks.text: PEP 8 — Python's style guide

items: Use **4 spaces** for indentation.
Name variables in `snake_case`, e.g. `total_price`.
Keep lines reasonably short (about 79–99 characters).
Put spaces around operators: `x = a + b`, not `x=a+b`.

blocks.text: Code is read far more often than it is written. Clean, commented code makes you look like a professional.

keyPoints: Triple quotes create docstrings for documentation.
Follow PEP 8: 4-space indents and snake_case names.
lessons.practice: Write a 3-line program and add a comment above each line explaining what it does.

lessons.title: Getting input from the user
lessons.summary: `input()` pauses the program, lets the user type something and returns it as a string.

blocks.text: Programs become interactive when they ask questions. `input()` shows an optional prompt and waits for the user to press enter.

blocks.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Nice to meet you,", name)
blocks.output:
What is your name? Saif
Nice to meet you, Saif

blocks.text: input() always returns text
Even if the user types a number, `input()` gives you a **string**. Convert it with `int()` or `float()` to do maths.

blocks.code:
age = input("Enter your age: ")
print(type(age))
age = int(age)
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
blocks.output:
Enter your age: 24
<class 'str'>
Next year you will be 25

blocks.text: In the PyMaster terminal, when a program calls `input()`, a yellow input bar appears under the console. Type and press enter.

keyPoints: `input(prompt)` reads a line of text from the user.
Use `int()` or `float()` to convert input to numbers.
lessons.practice: Ask for two numbers with `input()`, convert them with `int()` and print their sum.

lessons.title: Syntax, indentation & errors
lessons.summary: Python uses indentation to group code. Learn the rules and how to read error messages.

blocks.text: Many languages use `{ }` braces to group code. Python uses **indentation** — the spaces at the start of a line. Lines in the same block must have the same indentation (4 spaces is standard).

blocks.code:
temperature = 30
if temperature > 25:
    print("It's hot today")
    print("Drink water!")
print("This always runs")
blocks.output:
It's hot today
Drink water!
This always runs

blocks.text: Reading error messages
When something goes wrong Python shows a **traceback**. The last line tells you the error type and message; the lines above tell you where it happened.
A NameError — using a name that doesn't exist:
blocks.code:
print("Start")
print(undefined_name)
blocks.output:
Start
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(undefined_name)
          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
NameError: name 'undefined_name' is not defined

items: `SyntaxError` — code that breaks Python's grammar (missing `:` or bracket).
`IndentationError` — wrong or inconsistent indentation.
`NameError` — a variable or function name that doesn't exist.
`TypeError` — an operation on the wrong type, like `"5" + 5`.

blocks.text: Errors are normal! Professional developers read error messages carefully — they usually tell you exactly what to fix.

keyPoints: Tracebacks show where and why an error happened.
Read the last line of an error first.
lessons.practice: In the terminal, remove the indentation from a line inside an `if` block and read the error you get.

quiz.explain: Guido van Rossum released Python in 1991.

quiz.q: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?

options: It depends on what the user types

quiz.q: How many spaces does PEP 8 recommend for indentation?
Which error do you get when you use a variable that was never created?
quiz.explain: A `NameError` means Python doesn't know that name.

modules.title: Variables & Data Types
modules.subtitle: Store data with variables: numbers, text, booleans and None

lessons.title: Variables & naming rules
lessons.summary: A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory.

blocks.text: Create a variable with the **assignment operator** `=`. The name goes on the left, the value on the right.

blocks.code:
city = "Dhaka"
population = 23_000_000
is_capital = True
print(city, population, is_capital)

blocks.text: Variables can change. Python is **dynamically typed**, so a variable can even hold a different type later.

blocks.code:
score = 10
score = score + 5
print(score)
score = "fifteen"
print(score)

blocks.text: Naming rules

items: Must start with a letter or underscore: `name`, `_count`.
Can contain letters, numbers and underscores: `player2_score`.
Cannot start with a number: `2player` is invalid.
Case-sensitive: `Age` and `age` are different variables.
Don't use keywords like `if`, `for`, `class` as names.

blocks.text: Multiple assignment

blocks.code:
x, y, z = 1, 2, 3
a = b = 0
print(x, y, z, a, b)
x, y = y, x   # swap!
print(x, y)

blocks.text: Choose descriptive names: `total_price` is much clearer than `tp`.

keyPoints: `=` assigns a value to a variable.
Names are case-sensitive and use snake_case.
`a, b = b, a` swaps two values in one line.
lessons.practice: Create variables for your name, age and favourite language, then print a sentence using all three.

lessons.title: Numbers: int, float & complex
lessons.summary: Python has three numeric types and handles very large numbers easily.

items: `float` — decimal numbers: `3.14`, `-0.5`, `2.0`.
`complex` — numbers with an imaginary part: `2 + 3j` (used in science).

blocks.code:
a = 10
b = 3.5
c = 2 + 3j
print(type(a), type(b), type(c))
print(a + b)
print(2 ** 100)

blocks.text: Integers in Python have **unlimited size** — `2 ** 100` works perfectly.
Float precision
Floats are stored in binary, so some decimals can't be represented exactly.

blocks.code:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))
print(round(3.14159, 3))

blocks.text: Useful number functions

blocks.code:
print(abs(-7))
print(max(4, 9, 2), min(4, 9, 2))
print(pow(2, 5))
print(int(9.99), float(4))

blocks.text: Use `round()` when displaying money or measurements, or the `decimal` module for exact financial maths.

keyPoints: Python integers can be arbitrarily large.
Floats can have tiny rounding errors — use `round()` for display.
lessons.practice: Compute the area of a circle with radius 7 using `3.14159 * r ** 2` and round it to 2 decimals.

lessons.title: Strings basics
lessons.summary: Strings store text. They are one of the most used data types.

blocks.text: Create strings with single `'...'`, double `"..."` or triple quotes for multiple lines.

blocks.code:
first = "Ada"
last = 'Lovelace'
full = first + " " + last
print(full)
print(len(full))
print("ha" * 3)

blocks.text: `+` joins (concatenates) strings and `*` repeats them. `len()` returns the number of characters.
Indexing
Each character has a position (index) starting at **0**. Negative indexes count from the end.

blocks.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[0], word[1], word[-1])

blocks.text: f-strings
An **f-string** lets you put variables directly inside text using `{ }`. This is the modern, preferred way to format text.

blocks.code:
name = "Sara"
score = 92.456
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f} points")
print(f"2 + 3 = {2 + 3}")

blocks.text: Strings are **immutable** — you can't change a character in place, but you can create a new string.

keyPoints: Strings can use single, double or triple quotes.
Indexes start at 0; `-1` is the last character.
lessons.practice: Ask the user for their name and print it in uppercase along with its length using an f-string.

lessons.title: Booleans & None
lessons.summary: Booleans represent True or False. None represents 'no value'.

blocks.text: A **boolean** (`bool`) has only two values: `True` and `False`. They are the result of comparisons and drive decisions in code.

blocks.code:
is_logged_in = True
has_paid = False
print(type(is_logged_in))
print(10 > 5, 3 == 4)

blocks.text: Truthy and falsy values
Every value can be tested as a boolean. Empty or zero values are **falsy**; everything else is **truthy**.

blocks.code:
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool([]), bool(None))
print(bool(42), bool("hi"), bool([1, 2]))
blocks.output:
False False False False
True True True

blocks.text: None
`None` means 'nothing' or 'no value yet'. Functions that don't return anything return `None`.

blocks.code:
result = None
print(result)
print(result is None)

blocks.text: Compare with `None` using `is` or `is not`, not `==`.

keyPoints: Use `is None` to check for None.
lessons.practice: Print `bool()` of five different values and predict each result before running.

lessons.title: Type checking & conversion
lessons.summary: Find out a value's type and convert between types safely.

blocks.text: `type()` returns the type of a value. `isinstance()` checks whether a value is of a given type.

blocks.code:
values = [42, 3.5, "text", True, None, [1, 2]]
for v in values:
    print(repr(v), "->", type(v).__name__)
print(isinstance(42, int))
blocks.output:
42 -> int
3.5 -> float
'text' -> str
True -> bool
None -> NoneType
[1, 2] -> list
True

blocks.text: Converting types (casting)

blocks.code:
print(int("25") + 5)
print(float("2.5") * 2)
print(str(100) + " points")
print(int(7.9))
print(list("abc"))

blocks.text: Invalid conversions
Converting text that isn't a valid number raises a `ValueError`.

blocks.code: int("hello")
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 1, in <module>
    int("hello")
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'

blocks.text: You'll learn to handle these errors gracefully with `try`/`except` in Module 10.

keyPoints: `type(x)` shows the type, `isinstance(x, int)` tests it.
lessons.practice: Ask the user for a price as text, convert it to float, add 15% tax and print the total.

quiz.explain: Names can't start with a digit, contain `-`, or be keywords.

quiz.code:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
quiz.explain: `a, b = b, a` swaps the values.
The number `0` is falsy. Non-empty strings and lists are truthy.
Any number with a decimal point is a float.
`int()` can't parse a decimal string. Use `int(float("12.5"))`.

modules.title: Operators
modules.subtitle: Arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment and more

lessons.title: Arithmetic operators
lessons.summary: Do maths with Python: add, subtract, multiply, divide and more.

blocks.code:
a, b = 17, 5
print("a + b  =", a + b)
print("a - b  =", a - b)
print("a * b  =", a * b)
print("a / b  =", a / b)
print("a // b =", a // b)
print("a % b  =", a % b)
print("a ** 2 =", a ** 2)

items: `/` true division — always returns a float.
`//` floor division — divides and rounds down.
`%` modulo — the remainder after division.
`**` exponent — power.

blocks.text: Practical uses of % and //

blocks.code:
total_minutes = 135
hours = total_minutes // 60
minutes = total_minutes % 60
print(f"{hours}h {minutes}m")
print("Is 14 even?", 14 % 2 == 0)

blocks.text: `n % 2 == 0` is the classic way to test whether a number is even.

lessons.practice: Convert 1000 seconds into minutes and seconds using `//` and `%`.

lessons.title: Comparison operators
lessons.summary: Compare values to get True or False.

blocks.code:
x = 10
print(x == 10)
print(x != 5)
print(x > 3, x < 3)
print(x >= 10, x <= 9)
blocks.output:
True
True
True False
True False

blocks.text: Strings are compared alphabetically (by Unicode code). Uppercase letters come before lowercase.

blocks.code:
x = 10
print("apple" < "banana")
print("Zebra" < "apple")
print(1 < x < 20)

blocks.text: Python allows **chained comparisons** like `1 < x < 20` — very readable!
Don't confuse `=` (assignment) with `==` (comparison).

lessons.practice: Ask for an age and print whether it's between 13 and 19 using a chained comparison.

lessons.title: Logical operators
lessons.summary: Combine conditions with and, or and not.

items: `and` — True only if **both** sides are True.
`or` — True if **at least one** side is True.
`not` — flips True to False and vice versa.

blocks.code:
age = 22
has_ticket = True
print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age < 12 or age > 65)
print(not has_ticket)

blocks.text: Short-circuit evaluation
Python stops evaluating as soon as the result is known. `or` returns the first truthy value — handy for defaults.

blocks.code:
username = ""
display = username or "Guest"
print(display)
print(0 and 5, 3 and 5)

blocks.text: Precedence: `not` is evaluated first, then `and`, then `or`. Use parentheses to make intent clear.

keyPoints: `value or default` is a common pattern.
lessons.practice: Write a condition that is True when a number is positive AND even.

lessons.title: Assignment operators
lessons.summary: Shortcuts to update a variable using its current value.

blocks.code:
points = 10
points += 5
print(points)
points -= 3
print(points)
points *= 2
print(points)
points /= 4
print(points)
points //= 2
print(points)
points **= 3
print(points)

blocks.text: `x += 1` is the same as `x = x + 1`. These work with strings and lists too.

blocks.code:
message = "Hello"
message += ", World"
print(message)

blocks.text: Python has no `++` or `--` operators. Use `count += 1`.

lessons.practice: Start with `balance = 100`, add 50, subtract 30, double it and print it after each step.

lessons.title: Membership, identity & precedence
lessons.summary: Check if a value is inside a collection, whether two names point to the same object, and how Python orders operations.

blocks.text: Membership: in / not in

blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "mango", "kiwi"]
print("mango" in fruits)
print("grape" not in fruits)
print("py" in "python")

blocks.text: Identity: is / is not
`is` checks whether two variables refer to the **same object** in memory — not just equal values.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == c, a is c)
print(a is b)

blocks.text: Operator precedence
From highest to lowest: `**` → unary `-` → `* / // %` → `+ -` → comparisons → `not` → `and` → `or`.
When in doubt, add parentheses. They make code easier to read.

keyPoints: `in` tests membership in strings, lists, dicts…
`**` binds tighter than unary minus: `-2 ** 2` is `-4`.
lessons.practice: Check whether the letter `"z"` is in your name, and print the result.

quiz.explain: An empty string is falsy, so `or` returns the second value.

quiz.q: Which operator checks if two variables refer to the same object?

modules.title: Conditions
modules.subtitle: Make decisions with if, elif, else and match

lessons.title: The if statement
lessons.summary: Run code only when a condition is True.

blocks.text: An `if` statement checks a condition. If it's True, the indented block runs; otherwise it's skipped. Don't forget the colon `:` at the end of the line.

blocks.code:
battery = 15
if battery < 20:
    print("Low battery!")
    print("Please charge your phone.")
print("Check complete")
blocks.output:
Low battery!
Please charge your phone.
Check complete

blocks.text: Every line inside the block must be indented by the same amount (4 spaces).

keyPoints: `if condition:` followed by an indented block.
The block runs only when the condition is True.
lessons.practice: Ask for a temperature and print `"Wear a jacket"` if it is below 15.

lessons.title: if ... else
lessons.summary: Choose between two paths.

blocks.text: Conditional expression (ternary)
For simple choices you can write an if/else on one line.

blocks.code:
age = 20
status = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"
print(status)

keyPoints: `else:` runs when the `if` condition is False.
`x if condition else y` is a one-line conditional.
lessons.practice: Ask for a password and print `Access granted` if it equals `"python123"`, otherwise `Access denied`.

lessons.title: elif — multiple conditions
lessons.summary: Check several conditions in order; the first True one wins.

blocks.text: Python tests each condition from top to bottom and runs only the **first** matching block. Order matters!
Put the most specific (or highest) condition first.

keyPoints: Only the first True branch runs.
lessons.practice: Write a BMI category checker: Underweight (<18.5), Normal (<25), Overweight (<30), Obese.

lessons.title: Nested & combined conditions
lessons.summary: Put conditions inside conditions, or combine them with and/or.

blocks.text: Often the same logic is cleaner with logical operators:
Checking for empty values
Avoid deep nesting — flat code with `and`/`or`/`elif` is easier to read.

keyPoints: `if not items:` checks for empty collections.
lessons.practice: A shop gives 20% off to members who spend over 100, and 10% to everyone else over 100. Code it!

lessons.title: match-case (pattern matching)
lessons.summary: Python 3.10+ has a powerful match statement, similar to switch in other languages.

blocks.code:
command = "stop"
match command:
    case "start":
        print("Starting engine")
    case "stop":
        print("Stopping engine")
    case "pause" | "wait":
        print("Pausing")
    case _:
        print("Unknown command")

blocks.text: `case _:` is the wildcard — it matches anything, like `else`. `|` means 'or'.
Matching structures

blocks.code:
point = (0, 5)
match point:
    case (0, 0):
        print("Origin")
    case (0, y):
        print(f"On the Y axis at y={y}")
    case (x, 0):
        print(f"On the X axis at x={x}")
    case (x, y):
        print(f"Point at {x}, {y}")
blocks.output: On the Y axis at y=5

blocks.text: match-case shines when handling commands, menu options or structured data.

keyPoints: Patterns can capture values like `(0, y)`.
lessons.practice: Build a tiny menu: match `"1"`, `"2"`, `"3"` and print a different message for each.

quiz.explain: 15 is not > 20, but it is > 10, so the elif runs.

quiz.q: Which character must end an `if` line?
quiz.explain: Python blocks start after a colon.
`0` is falsy, so the else value is used.
The underscore is the wildcard pattern.

quiz.q: How many `elif` blocks can an `if` statement have?
quiz.explain: You can chain any number of `elif` blocks.
Only the first matching branch runs.

modules.title: Loops
modules.subtitle: Repeat work with for and while loops

lessons.title: for loops & range()
lessons.summary: A for loop repeats code once for every item in a sequence.

blocks.code:
for i in range(5):
    print("Iteration", i)

blocks.text: `range(stop)` produces numbers from 0 up to (but **not including**) `stop`. You can also pass a start and a step.

blocks.code:
print(list(range(1, 6)))
print(list(range(0, 20, 5)))
print(list(range(10, 0, -2)))

blocks.text: Multiplication table
`range(1, 11)` gives 1 to 10 — the end value is always excluded.

keyPoints: `for item in sequence:` repeats for each item.
Use a negative step to count down.
lessons.practice: Print all even numbers from 2 to 30 using `range()` with a step.

lessons.title: while loops
lessons.summary: A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays True.

blocks.code:
countdown = 5
while countdown > 0:
    print(countdown)
    countdown -= 1
print("Happy New Year! 🎉")

blocks.text: Make sure something inside the loop eventually makes the condition False, or you'll create an **infinite loop**.
Loop until valid input

blocks.code:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("Password: ")
print("Welcome in!")
blocks.output:
Password: java
Password: 1234
Password: python
Welcome in!

blocks.text: Stuck in an infinite loop in the terminal? Tap **Stop** to interrupt it.

keyPoints: `while condition:` loops while the condition is True.
Update variables inside the loop to avoid infinite loops.
lessons.practice: Keep asking for numbers and add them up until the user types 0, then print the total.

lessons.title: break, continue & else
lessons.summary: Control the flow of a loop from the inside.

items: `break` — exit the loop immediately.
`continue` — skip the rest of this iteration and move to the next.
`else` on a loop — runs only if the loop finished **without** `break`.

blocks.text: Search with for ... else
Infinite loop with break

blocks.code:
total = 0
while True:
    value = int(input("Number (0 to stop): "))
    if value == 0:
        break
    total += value
print("Total:", total)
blocks.output:
Number (0 to stop): 5
Number (0 to stop): 10
Number (0 to stop): 0
Total: 15

keyPoints: `break` exits, `continue` skips to the next iteration.
lessons.practice: Print numbers 1–50 but skip multiples of 3 and stop completely at the first multiple of 17.

lessons.title: Nested loops & patterns
lessons.summary: Put a loop inside another loop to work with grids and patterns.

blocks.text: Star pyramid
The inner loop runs completely for every single iteration of the outer loop.

keyPoints: Great for grids, tables and patterns.
lessons.practice: Print a 5×5 multiplication grid with numbers aligned using f-string width formatting.

lessons.title: Looping like a pro: enumerate & zip
lessons.summary: Pythonic tools that make loops cleaner.

blocks.text: enumerate() — index and value
zip() — loop over several lists together

blocks.code:
names = ["Ali", "Sara", "John"]
scores = [88, 95, 72]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name:<6}{score}")

blocks.text: Looping over a dictionary

blocks.output:
apples: in stock
pears: sold out
plums: in stock

blocks.text: Useful helpers

blocks.code:
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
print(sum(nums), sorted(nums), list(reversed(nums)))

lessons.practice: Use `zip()` to print each student with their grade from two lists.

quiz.q: When does a loop's `else` block run?
options: Only when the loop never runs
quiz.explain: `else` is skipped if the loop was exited with `break`.

quiz.q: How many times does the inner print run?
What is the risk of `while True:` without `break`?
quiz.explain: Without a `break`, the loop never ends.

modules.title: Functions
modules.subtitle: Write reusable code with def, parameters and return

lessons.title: Defining & calling functions
lessons.summary: Functions package code under a name so you can reuse it.

blocks.code:
def greet():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Welcome to PyMaster")

greet()
greet()
blocks.output:
Hello!
Welcome to PyMaster
Hello!
Welcome to PyMaster

blocks.text: `def` defines a function. The code inside doesn't run until you **call** it with parentheses.
Why functions?

items: **Reuse** — write once, use many times.
**Organize** — split big programs into small named pieces.
**Test** — small functions are easy to check.

blocks.text: Name functions with verbs in snake_case: `calculate_total`, `send_email`.

keyPoints: Functions make code reusable and organized.
lessons.practice: Write a function `print_banner()` that prints a 3-line welcome banner, then call it twice.

lessons.title: Parameters & return values
lessons.summary: Pass data in with parameters and get results back with return.

blocks.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 4)
print(result)
print(add(10, 20) * 2)

blocks.text: `return` sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. Without `return`, a function returns `None`.

blocks.output:
A 4x5 room is 20 m²
A 2x3 room is 6 m²
None

blocks.text: Returning several values

keyPoints: Return several values as a tuple.
lessons.practice: Write `celsius_to_fahrenheit(c)` that returns `c * 9 / 5 + 32` and print it for 0, 25 and 100.

lessons.title: Default & keyword arguments
lessons.summary: Make functions flexible and easy to call.

blocks.code:
def make_coffee(size="medium", sugar=1, milk=True):
    milk_text = "with milk" if milk else "black"
    return f"{size} coffee, {sugar} sugar, {milk_text}"

print(make_coffee())
print(make_coffee("large"))
print(make_coffee(sugar=0, milk=False))
blocks.output:
medium coffee, 1 sugar, with milk
large coffee, 1 sugar, with milk
medium coffee, 0 sugar, black

blocks.text: Default values are used when an argument isn't passed. **Keyword arguments** (`sugar=0`) can be given in any order.
Never use a mutable default like `def f(items=[])` — use `items=None` and create the list inside.

lessons.practice: Write `power(base, exp=2)` and call it with and without the exponent.

lessons.title: *args and **kwargs
lessons.summary: Accept any number of positional or keyword arguments.

blocks.text: `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a **tuple**. `**kwargs` collects keyword arguments into a **dictionary**.

blocks.output:
Name: Saif
  role: Developer
  language: Python

blocks.text: Unpacking when calling

blocks.code:
def point(x, y, z):
    return f"({x}, {y}, {z})"

coords = [1, 2, 3]
print(point(*coords))
print(point(**{"x": 4, "y": 5, "z": 6}))

lessons.practice: Write `average(*nums)` that returns the average of any amount of numbers.

lessons.title: Scope & lambda functions
lessons.summary: Understand where variables live, and write tiny anonymous functions.

blocks.text: Local vs global scope

blocks.code:
message = "global"

def show():
    message = "local"
    print("Inside:", message)

show()
print("Outside:", message)

blocks.text: Variables created inside a function are **local** — they disappear when the function ends. Use `global` only when you really need to change a global variable.

blocks.code:
counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

increment()
increment()
print(counter)

blocks.text: lambda — small anonymous functions

blocks.code:
square = lambda x: x * x
print(square(6))

people = [("Ali", 31), ("Sara", 24), ("John", 28)]
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])
print(people)

blocks.text: lambda is perfect as a `key` for `sorted()`, `max()` and `min()`.

keyPoints: Local variables live only inside their function.
`global` lets a function change a global variable.
`lambda args: expression` creates a small function.
lessons.practice: Sort a list of words by their length using `sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w))`.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.summary: A function that calls itself to solve smaller versions of a problem.

blocks.text: Every recursive function needs a **base case** that stops the recursion, otherwise it calls itself forever.

blocks.code:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Lift off!")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)

countdown(3)

blocks.text: Python limits recursion depth (about 1000 calls). For big inputs a loop is often better.

keyPoints: Loops can replace recursion for large inputs.
lessons.practice: Write a recursive `sum_to(n)` that returns 1 + 2 + … + n.

quiz.q: What does a function return if it has no `return` statement?
What does `(lambda x: x * 3)(4)` evaluate to?
What is the base case in recursion?
quiz.explain: Without a base case, recursion never ends.

quiz.code:
x = 1
def change():
    x = 5
change()
print(x)
quiz.explain: The function changes only its local `x`.

modules.title: Collections
modules.subtitle: Lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries and comprehensions

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.summary: Ordered, changeable collections — the workhorse of Python.

blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0], fruits[-1])
fruits[1] = "blueberry"
print(fruits)
print(len(fruits))

blocks.text: Adding and removing

blocks.code:
tasks = ["code"]
tasks.append("test")
tasks.insert(0, "plan")
tasks.extend(["deploy", "relax"])
print(tasks)
tasks.remove("relax")
last = tasks.pop()
print(last, tasks)

blocks.text: Lists can hold mixed types: `[1, "two", 3.0, True]`, and even other lists.

keyPoints: Lists are ordered and mutable: `[a, b, c]`.
lessons.practice: Create a shopping list, add 3 items, remove 1 and print the final list with its length.

lessons.title: List slicing & methods
lessons.summary: Slice lists and use built-in methods to sort, search and count.

blocks.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
print(nums[1:4])
print(nums[:3])
print(nums[3:])
print(nums[::2])
print(nums[::-1])

blocks.text: Slicing uses `[start:stop:step]` — like `range()`, `stop` is excluded.

blocks.code:
scores = [72, 95, 88, 61, 95]
scores.sort()
print(scores)
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)
print(scores.count(95), scores.index(88))
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))

blocks.text: Copying lists

blocks.code:
original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original
copy = original.copy()
original.append(4)
print(alias, copy)

blocks.text: `b = a` doesn't copy a list — both names point to the same list. Use `.copy()` or `a[:]`.

lessons.practice: Given a list of 10 numbers, print the first 3, the last 3 and every second number.

lessons.title: Tuples
lessons.summary: Ordered collections that can't be changed after creation.

blocks.code:
point = (3, 4)
rgb = (255, 128, 0)
print(point[0], rgb[-1])
print(len(rgb))

blocks.text: Tuples are **immutable**: you can't add, remove or change items. They're perfect for fixed data like coordinates or dates.
Trying to change a tuple raises an error:
blocks.code:
colors = ("red", "green")
colors[0] = "blue"
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    colors[0] = "blue"
    ~~~~~~^^^
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

blocks.text: Tuple unpacking

blocks.code:
person = ("Sara", 28, "Engineer")
name, age, job = person
print(f"{name} is a {age}-year-old {job}")
single = (5,)
print(type(single))

blocks.text: A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`.

lessons.practice: Store a date as `(day, month, year)` and print it as `day/month/year` using unpacking.

lessons.title: Sets
lessons.summary: Unordered collections of unique items with powerful maths operations.

blocks.code:
tags = {"python", "code", "python", "ai"}
print(len(tags))
tags.add("web")
tags.discard("code")
print("ai" in tags)

blocks.text: Sets automatically remove duplicates — a quick way to get unique values from a list.

blocks.code:
emails = ["a@x.com", "b@x.com", "a@x.com"]
print(sorted(set(emails)))

blocks.text: Set operations
Checking `x in my_set` is extremely fast, even for huge sets.

lessons.practice: Find the common letters in two words using a set intersection.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.summary: Store data as key → value pairs for fast lookups.

blocks.code:
student = {"name": "Ali", "age": 21, "major": "CS"}
print(student["name"])
student["age"] = 22
student["gpa"] = 3.8
print(student)

blocks.text: Safe access and methods

blocks.code:
student = {"name": "Ali", "age": 22}
print(student.get("email", "not set"))
print(list(student.keys()))
print(list(student.values()))
removed = student.pop("age")
print(removed, student)

blocks.text: Counting with a dictionary
Nested data

blocks.output:
u1 Sara Python, SQL
u2 John Kotlin

blocks.text: Dictionary keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples) and unique.

lessons.practice: Build a phone book dictionary with 3 contacts and print each name with its number.

lessons.title: Comprehensions
lessons.summary: Build lists, sets and dictionaries in a single expressive line.

blocks.code:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 8)]
print(squares)
evens = [n for n in range(20) if n % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

blocks.text: A **list comprehension** has the form `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`.

blocks.code:
words = ["python", "is", "awesome"]
print([w.upper() for w in words])
print({w: len(w) for w in words})
print({len(w) for w in words})

blocks.text: With if-else

blocks.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(["even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd" for n in nums])

blocks.text: Keep comprehensions short. If it gets hard to read, use a normal loop.

keyPoints: `[expr for x in items if cond]` builds a list.
`{k: v for ...}` builds a dict, `{x for ...}` a set.
lessons.practice: Create a list of the cubes of all odd numbers from 1 to 15 with a comprehension.

quiz.q: Which collection does NOT allow duplicates?
What does `d.get("x", 0)` return if `"x"` is missing?

modules.title: Working with Strings
modules.subtitle: String methods, slicing, formatting and text processing

lessons.title: String methods
lessons.summary: Python strings come with dozens of handy built-in methods.

blocks.code:
text = "  Hello, Python World!  "
print(text.strip())
print(text.lower())
print(text.upper())
print(text.strip().title())
print(text.replace("World", "Developers"))
blocks.output:
Hello, Python World!
  hello, python world!  
  HELLO, PYTHON WORLD!  
Hello, Python World!
  Hello, Python Developers!

blocks.text: Searching

blocks.code:
s = "learning python is fun"
print(s.startswith("learn"), s.endswith("!"))
print(s.find("python"), s.find("java"))
print(s.count("n"))

blocks.text: Checking content

blocks.code:
print("12345".isdigit(), "abc".isalpha(), "abc123".isalnum())
print("   ".isspace(), "Hello".istitle())

blocks.text: String methods return **new** strings — the original stays the same.

lessons.practice: Ask for a username, strip spaces, make it lowercase and check that it contains only letters and numbers.

lessons.title: Split, join & slicing
lessons.summary: Break text into parts, put it back together and cut out pieces.

blocks.code:
sentence = "Python is easy to learn"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)
print(len(words))
csv_line = "Ali,25,Dhaka"
print(csv_line.split(","))

words = ["Python", "Kotlin", "Swift"]
print(", ".join(words))
print(" -> ".join(words))
blocks.output:
Python, Kotlin, Swift
Python -> Kotlin -> Swift

blocks.text: Slicing strings

blocks.code:
code = "PYM-2026-ABCD"
print(code[:3])
print(code[4:8])
print(code[-4:])
print("racecar"[::-1])

blocks.text: `text[::-1]` reverses a string — great for checking palindromes.

keyPoints: `split(sep)` turns a string into a list.
`sep.join(list)` turns a list into a string.
lessons.practice: Check whether a word typed by the user is a palindrome.

lessons.title: f-strings & formatting
lessons.summary: Format numbers, align columns and build professional output.

blocks.code:
name, price, qty = "Laptop", 1299.5, 3
print(f"{name} costs ${price:,.2f}")
print(f"Total: {price * qty:,.2f}")
print(f"{0.4567:.1%}")
print(f"{42:05d}")

blocks.text: Alignment

blocks.code:
items = [("Coffee", 3.5), ("Sandwich", 7.25), ("Juice", 4)]
print(f"{'Item':<12}{'Price':>8}")
print("-" * 20)
for item, cost in items:
    print(f"{item:<12}{cost:>8.2f}")

items: `:<10` left-align, `:>10` right-align, `:^10` centre in 10 characters.
`:.2f` two decimal places, `:,` thousands separator, `:%` percentage.

blocks.text: Debugging with =

keyPoints: `f"{x=}"` prints name and value — great for debugging.
lessons.practice: Print a neat receipt with three items, aligned prices and a total.

lessons.title: Escape characters & multiline text
lessons.summary: Special characters, raw strings and long text.

blocks.code:
print("Line 1\nLine 2")
print("Name:\tSaif")
print("She said \"Hi!\"")
print('It\'s Python')
print("Back\\slash")
blocks.output:
Line 1
Line 2
Name:	Saif
She said "Hi!"
It's Python
Back\slash

items: `\n` new line, `\t` tab, `\\` backslash, `\"` quote.

blocks.text: Multiline strings

blocks.code:
poem = """Roses are red,
Python is neat,
Indentation matters,
And code is complete."""
print(poem)
blocks.output:
Roses are red,
Python is neat,
Indentation matters,
And code is complete.

blocks.text: Raw strings

blocks.code:
path = r"C:\new\test"
print(path)

blocks.text: Use raw strings `r"..."` for Windows paths and regular expressions.

keyPoints: Escape sequences start with a backslash.
lessons.practice: Print a small table using `\t` tabs between columns.

lessons.title: Text processing in practice
lessons.summary: Combine everything to analyse real text.

blocks.code:
text = """Python is powerful. Python is friendly.
Python is fast to learn and fun to use."""

words = text.lower().replace(".", "").split()
print("Words:", len(words))
print("Unique:", len(set(words)))

freq = {}
for w in words:
    freq[w] = freq.get(w, 0) + 1
top = sorted(freq.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:3]
for word, count in top:
    print(f"{word:<10}{count}")

blocks.text: Simple validation

blocks.output:
saif@mail.com -> True
bad.email -> False
a b@x.com -> False

blocks.text: For complex patterns, learn the `re` (regular expressions) module next.

keyPoints: Normalize text with `lower()` and `replace()` before analysing.
Dictionaries are perfect for counting words.

quiz.explain: join puts the separator between items.
A step of -1 reverses the string.

modules.title: File Handling
modules.subtitle: Read and write files, CSV, JSON and paths

lessons.title: Writing files
lessons.summary: Save data permanently by writing it to a file.

blocks.text: `open(filename, mode)` opens a file. Mode `"w"` **writes** (creating or overwriting the file), `"a"` **appends** to the end.

blocks.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Python notes\n")
    f.write("1. Variables\n")
    f.write("2. Loops\n")
print("File written!")

blocks.text: Appending

blocks.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Day 1: started Python\n")
with open("notes.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Day 2: learned loops\n")
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
blocks.output:
Day 1: started Python
Day 2: learned loops

blocks.text: In the PyMaster terminal files are saved in a private sandbox folder inside the app.

keyPoints: `write()` doesn't add new lines — include `\n` yourself.
lessons.practice: Write a file `todo.txt` with three tasks, one per line.

lessons.title: Reading files
lessons.summary: Load text back from a file in different ways.

blocks.code:
with open("fruits.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("apple\nbanana\ncherry\n")

with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    content = f.read()
print(repr(content))

with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print("->", line.strip())

with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
print(lines)

items: `read()` — the whole file as one string.
`for line in f` — one line at a time (memory-friendly for big files).
`readlines()` — a list of all lines.

blocks.text: Missing files

blocks.code: open("does_not_exist.txt")
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 1, in <module>
    open("does_not_exist.txt")
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'does_not_exist.txt'

lessons.practice: Write 5 numbers to a file, then read them back and print their sum.

lessons.title: The with statement
lessons.summary: Context managers close files automatically — even when errors happen.

blocks.text: Files must be closed after use. `with` does it for you when the block ends.

blocks.code:
f = open("demo.txt", "w")
f.write("manual")
f.close()
print("closed:", f.closed)

with open("demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
print("closed:", f.closed)

blocks.text: Encoding
Always specify `encoding="utf-8"` when working with text that may contain non-English characters or emoji.

blocks.code:
with open("hello.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello 👋 আসসালামু আলাইকুম")
with open("hello.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

blocks.text: Always prefer `with open(...)` — it's the professional standard.

lessons.practice: Use `with` to copy the contents of one file into another file.

lessons.title: CSV & JSON files
lessons.summary: Work with the two most common data formats.

blocks.text: CSV — spreadsheet data

blocks.code:
import csv

rows = [["name", "score"], ["Ali", 88], ["Sara", 95]]
with open("scores.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows(rows)

with open("scores.csv") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], "scored", row["score"])

blocks.text: JSON — structured data

blocks.code:
import json

profile = {"name": "Saif", "skills": ["Python", "Kotlin"], "level": 3}
with open("profile.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(profile, f, indent=2)

with open("profile.json") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)
print(loaded["skills"])
print(json.dumps(loaded))

blocks.text: JSON is how most web APIs send data — learning it is essential.

lessons.practice: Save a list of 3 books (title, author) as JSON, then load and print them.

lessons.title: os & pathlib
lessons.summary: Work with folders, paths and file information.

blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("projects")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(folder / "app.py").write_text("print('hi')")
(folder / "readme.md").write_text("# Readme")

for item in sorted(folder.iterdir()):
    print(item.name, item.suffix, item.stat().st_size, "bytes")
print((folder / "app.py").exists())

import os

os.makedirs("data/logs", exist_ok=True)
print(os.path.join("data", "logs", "today.txt"))
print(os.path.exists("data/logs"))
print(os.path.splitext("photo.jpeg"))

blocks.text: `pathlib` is the modern, object-oriented way to handle paths. `/` joins path parts.

lessons.practice: Create a folder with 3 text files, then list only the `.txt` files with `glob("*.txt")`.

quiz.q: Which mode adds text to the end of an existing file?
What is the main benefit of `with open(...)`?
quiz.explain: The context manager closes the file for you.

quiz.q: Which error is raised when opening a missing file for reading?
Which function converts a Python dict into a JSON string?

modules.title: Errors & Exceptions
modules.subtitle: Handle problems gracefully with try, except, finally and raise

lessons.title: Common error types
lessons.summary: Know the errors you'll meet most often and what causes them.

items: `SyntaxError` — invalid Python grammar.
`NameError` — unknown variable name.
`TypeError` — wrong type, e.g. `"2" + 2`.
`ValueError` — right type, wrong value, e.g. `int("abc")`.
`IndexError` — list index out of range.
`KeyError` — missing dictionary key.
`ZeroDivisionError` — dividing by zero.
`AttributeError` — the object has no such attribute/method.

blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
print(numbers[5])
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(numbers[5])
          ~~~~~~~^^^
IndexError: list index out of range

blocks.code: total = "Score: " + 100
blocks.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 1, in <module>
    total = "Score: " + 100
            ~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

blocks.text: Read the error type and message first — they point straight at the problem.

keyPoints: Each error type tells you what went wrong.
lessons.practice: Trigger a KeyError on purpose using a dictionary, and read the message.

lessons.title: try & except
lessons.summary: Catch errors so your program keeps running.

blocks.output:
Your age: twenty
Please type a whole number!

blocks.text: Several except blocks

blocks.output:
5.0
Cannot divide by zero
Numbers only, please

blocks.text: Getting the error message
Catch specific exceptions. A bare `except:` hides bugs.

keyPoints: `try:` code that might fail, `except Type:` handles it.
Use several except blocks for different errors.
`except Error as e` gives you the error object.
lessons.practice: Keep asking for a number until the user enters a valid integer (use while + try/except).

lessons.title: else & finally
lessons.summary: Run code only on success, or always — no matter what.

blocks.output:
Got 3.5
-- check done --
'abc' is not a number
-- check done --

items: `else` runs only if **no** exception happened.
`finally` runs **always** — perfect for cleanup like closing connections.

keyPoints: `finally` = always runs, even after errors or return.
lessons.practice: Write a function that opens a file and uses `finally` to print "closing".

lessons.title: Raising exceptions
lessons.summary: Signal problems in your own code with raise.

blocks.text: assert for sanity checks

blocks.output:
4.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 6, in <module>
    average([])
  File "main.py", line 2, in average
    assert len(nums) > 0, "list must not be empty"
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError: list must not be empty

blocks.text: Raise exceptions early when input is invalid — it makes bugs easy to find.

lessons.practice: Write `set_age(age)` that raises ValueError if age is negative or above 150.

lessons.title: Custom exceptions
lessons.summary: Create your own exception classes for clearer error handling.

blocks.output:
Payment failed: You need 30 more
Missing amount: 30

blocks.text: Custom exceptions inherit from `Exception`. They make your code self-documenting and let callers catch exactly what they need.
Name custom exceptions with the `Error` suffix, like `ValidationError`.

keyPoints: Inherit from `Exception` to make your own error type.
lessons.practice: Create `InvalidEmailError` and raise it from a `register(email)` function.

quiz.explain: Right type (str), but an invalid value for int.

quiz.code:
try:
    1 / 0
    print("A")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("B")
finally:
    print("C")
quiz.explain: The ZeroDivisionError is caught, then finally runs.

quiz.q: Which keyword triggers an exception yourself?

modules.title: Object-Oriented Programming
modules.subtitle: Classes, objects, inheritance and dunder methods

lessons.title: Classes & objects
lessons.summary: A class is a blueprint; objects are things built from it.

blocks.code:
class Car:
    pass

my_car = Car()
my_car.brand = "Toyota"
print(type(my_car).__name__, my_car.brand)

blocks.text: A **class** defines a new type. An **object** (instance) is created by calling the class like a function. Objects bundle **data** (attributes) and **behaviour** (methods).

items: Class: `Dog` — the idea of a dog.
Objects: `rex`, `bella` — specific dogs with their own names and ages.

blocks.text: Class names use `CapWords` (PascalCase): `BankAccount`, `HttpClient`.

lessons.practice: Create an empty class `Book`, make two objects and give each a `title` attribute.

lessons.title: __init__ & attributes
lessons.summary: Initialize every new object with its own data.

blocks.code:
class Student:
    school = "PyMaster Academy"   # class attribute (shared)

    def __init__(self, name, grade):
        self.name = name          # instance attributes
        self.grade = grade

a = Student("Ali", 90)
b = Student("Sara", 95)
print(a.name, a.grade, a.school)
print(b.name, b.grade, b.school)
blocks.output:
Ali 90 PyMaster Academy
Sara 95 PyMaster Academy

blocks.text: `__init__` runs automatically when an object is created. `self` refers to the object being built.
Instance attributes belong to one object; class attributes are shared by all objects.

lessons.practice: Create a `Rectangle` class with `width` and `height` set in `__init__`.

lessons.title: Methods & self
lessons.summary: Give objects behaviour with methods.

blocks.code:
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            print("Insufficient funds")
            return self.balance
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance

acc = BankAccount("Saif", 100)
acc.deposit(50)
acc.withdraw(500)
acc.withdraw(30)
print(acc.owner, acc.balance)

blocks.text: A **generator** function uses `yield` instead of `return`. It pauses after each value and resumes when the next value is requested.
Generator expressions `( ... )` handle millions of items using almost no memory.

blocks.text: `@shout` is the same as writing `greet = shout(greet)`. Decorators are used everywhere — Flask routes, logging, timing, caching.
`functools.lru_cache` is a built-in decorator that can make recursive functions dramatically faster.

keyPoints: A decorator takes a function and returns a new one.

lessons.title: Context managers
lessons.summary: Set up and clean up resources reliably with with.

blocks.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def section(title):
    print(f"=== {title} ===")
    yield
    print("=" * (len(title) + 8))

with section("Report"):
    print("Sales: 120")
    print("Users: 45")
